headline: Showers Monday, then a Tuesday night–Wednesday front brings lowland rain, first notable Cascade snow, and a cooler weekend.
summary: As of Sunday evening, a low off the coast is drifting south and will move onto northwest Oregon by Monday afternoon, weakening as it goes. Until then western Washington gets periodic showers, with steadier rain at times over the Cascades and coast. Highs Monday stay in the 50s for most areas. Snow falls only on high mountains, with the snow level near 5000 feet in heavier showers. Winds are easing tonight along the coast and around Admiralty Inlet. Tuesday stays unsettled, with a few Cascade showers and highs in the mid 50s. A new front arrives from British Columbia late Tuesday into Tuesday night, bringing more rain and locally breezy winds, and colder air as it crosses the region into Wednesday. Forecasters call it the first noticeable mountain snow event of the season. Snow levels during the heaviest precipitation are 3500 to 4500 feet, so the higher Cascade passes could get snow, mostly Tuesday evening into early Wednesday. Snow amounts are uncertain: the odds of more than 6 inches in 24 hours ending 5 PM Wednesday are about 90% at Paradise and 70% at Heather Meadows (Mt. Baker), but only 20% at Stevens Pass and 15% at Rainy Pass. Lowlands get rain Wednesday, with a small (15%) chance of thunderstorms for most areas. The low behind the front deepens offshore Thursday and lingers off Washington and Oregon into late week, keeping things unsettled. By late Friday into the weekend the storm track is expected to shift farther south, which should reduce the chance of precipitation. Temperatures turn cooler over the weekend, and forecasters will watch for frost or freeze in the mornings. No watches, warnings, or advisories are in effect for land areas; forecasters are still considering whether the Cascade snow will need a winter weather headline.
changes: Earlier discussions expected light snow of about 4 inches at the passes midweek and a Tuesday arrival; the evening update shifts the focus to Tuesday night–Wednesday, gives snow levels of 3500 to 4500 feet, and adds uneven snow odds, a 15% lowland thunderstorm chance, and frost or freeze watching for the weekend. It also expects the storm track to shift south by late Friday, replacing the earlier note that Saturday was uncertain.
